item.title: World Rabies Day: What pet owners need to know
item.description:
Picture yourself at home, focused on your computer, when your playful dog or cat jumps onto your desk and nips your hand while playing.
For many pet owners, such bites or scratches may appear harmless, but veterinarians warn that even minor injuries can pose a serious health risk if the animal has not been vaccinated against rabies.
“People often ignore these incidents because they consider their pets harmless,” Dr Abdul Aziz Al Mamun, director of the Central Veterinary Hospital in Dhaka, told the Dhaka Tribune.
He advised pet owners to keep a safe distance from animals that show signs of agitation, noting that even familiar pets can bite or scratch unexpectedly.
He also stressed that regular vaccination and proper care are fundamental to preventing rabies.
The warning comes as the number of people seeking treatment after animal bites continues to rise in Bangladesh, while rabies deaths are still being reported.
According to the Infectious Diseases Hospital in Dhaka, 146,243 people sought outpatient treatment after animal bites in 2025, compared with 122,263 in 2024.
By September 17 this year, around 107,000 people had already sought treatment.
As Bangladesh observes World Rabies Day 2026 on Monday, veterinarians and public health officials are urging pet owners to take greater responsibility for vaccination and animal care.
Pet owners should ensure their dogs and cats receive rabies vaccinations on the schedule recommended by veterinarians.
Keeping a pet indoors does not by itself eliminate the risk of rabies.
Vaccination protects the animal and reduces the potential risk to people who come into contact with it.
Owners should also keep vaccination records and consult a veterinarian about booster doses and other preventive care.
Department of Livestock Services Director (Extension) Dr Begum Shamsunnahar Ahmed said vaccination is essential to preventing the spread of rabies.
“There is no alternative to vaccinating animals,” she said.
She also called for stray dogs and cats to be vaccinated rather than killed, saying vaccination is an important tool for breaking the transmission cycle.
She warned people not to dismiss a bite or scratch simply because it came from a familiar pet.
The wound should be washed immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water, after which the injured person should seek medical attention as soon as possible.
Doctors will assess the nature of the exposure and the animal involved to determine whether rabies vaccination or rabies immunoglobulin is required.
Dr Shamsunnahar urged people not to rely on traditional remedies following an animal bite.
“Do not depend on faith healing (jhar-fuk), water or ointments. The wound must be washed with soap and water and medical attention should be sought quickly,” she said.
Veterinarians say even normally friendly dogs and cats can behave unpredictably when frightened, disturbed while eating, protecting their young or responding to sudden movements.
Dr Abdul Aziz advised pet owners to remain alert and give animals adequate space when they appear agitated.
Children should also be taught not to tease or provoke pets, particularly while the animals are eating, sleeping or caring for their young.
Although dogs remain the main source of human rabies infections, health workers are increasingly seeing patients seeking treatment after cat bites and scratches.
A doctor at the Infectious Diseases Hospital said many of the patients arriving at the vaccination center had been attacked by cats.
She said many pet owners do not vaccinate their cats and that incidents involving cat bites and scratches have increased over the past 3-4 years.
The growing popularity of pet cats has added another dimension to the country's rabies prevention efforts, particularly in urban areas.
The increase in animal-bite cases is a concern because rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms develop.
Bangladesh recorded 58 rabies deaths in 2024 and 59 in 2025, while 35 deaths were reported during the first 2.5 months of this year, according to information provided by health authorities.
The Directorate General of Health Services does not maintain comprehensive nationwide data on the total number of people bitten by dogs and cats.
Globally, the World Health Organization estimates that rabies causes around 59,000 deaths each year, with dogs responsible for about 99% of human rabies infections.
However, rabies is preventable if people receive appropriate post-exposure treatment promptly after a potentially risky bite or scratch.
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku said greater awareness, wider animal vaccination and timely treatment could significantly reduce rabies infections and deaths in Bangladesh.
“Prevention is more important than controlling the disease after it occurs,” he said at a World Rabies Day discussion in Dhaka on Monday.
He called for stronger rabies prevention activities in both urban and rural areas, particularly where awareness remains low.
Bangladesh has run an integrated rabies control program since 2010, covering dog vaccination, population control, public awareness and treatment for people exposed to the virus.
According to DGHS data, the program vaccinated around 2.9 million dogs in more than 60 districts.
The first round of vaccination was completed in all 64 districts, while subsequent rounds covered fewer districts.
Officials involved in disease-control activities have said the program effectively stalled after the change of government in 2024, with funding shortages preventing renewed dog vaccination and population-control campaigns.
DLS Director General Md Shahjahan Khan said dog vaccination and population-control programs should be expanded nationwide rather than being concentrated in Dhaka.
For Dhaka's growing community of pet owners, veterinarians say rabies prevention begins with responsible pet ownership: keeping vaccinations up to date, understanding an animal's behavior, avoiding situations that may trigger bites or scratches and seeking medical attention promptly after any potentially risky exposure.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,099 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Monday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,099.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 998, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 101, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the three new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in the Chittagong division, with two deaths. At the district level, one casualty each was recorded in Chittagong, Noakhali, and Sylhet.
A total of 1,214 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Monday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 189,255.
During the same period, 96 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 21,308.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 167,469 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 160,705 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Monday said there is no hidden agenda behind the latest agreement with Boeing, reiterating that Bangladesh will continue to expand Biman’s fleet based on needs as the country eyes becoming an aviation hub.
"We need to expand the fleet to become an aviation hub. There is nothing....there is no hidden agenda. Bangladesh does it on the basis of needs. We need to expand our fleet," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs while responding to a question.
Kobir laid emphasis on a mixed fleet in the interest of the country’s aviation sector.
The state minister described the just-concluded visit of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to the 81st session of the UNGA as "successful and meaningful," with extensive engagements with the international community during his four-day stay in New York.
Kobir said the speech of the prime minister at the UNGA was highly appreciated by the international community.
Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the country's national flag carrier, signed an agreement with US aircraft manufacturer Boeing to acquire 11 additional aircraft during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
"Congratulations to Boeing and Biman on the agreement to purchase 11 more of the world’s best commercial planes. Another win-win for the US-Bangladesh relationship! Will be tuning in to the signing ceremony in New York later," said US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T Christensen moments before the signing ceremony.

The deadline for online applications in the second phase of Class XI admissions for the 2026-27 academic year has been extended to 8pm on October 1.
The schedules for the publication of second-phase results, selection confirmation, migration and final admission have also been revised.
The revised schedule was announced in a notice signed by Professor Dr Syed Akhtaruzzaman, president of the Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and chairman of the Dhaka Education Board, on Monday.
According to the notice, the schedule was revised to address complications caused by a large number of students failing to cancel their selections or complete the admission process within the stipulated time.
Students who did not apply earlier, were not selected by any college despite applying, received a nomination but failed to confirm their selection or complete admission, or were unable to secure admission due to incorrect quota selection can apply in the second phase.
Under the revised schedule, the second-phase results will be published at 8pm on October 5.
Selection confirmation will remain open until 8pm on October 8. Applications and selections will be cancelled if students fail to confirm their selections within the deadline.
Migration results will be published at 8pm on October 9, while final admission will be held from October 11 to 13.

item.title: Embassy issues travel advisory for Bangladeshis visiting Nepal
item.description:
The Embassy of Bangladesh in Kathmandu on Sunday night urged Bangladeshi tourists and trekkers to exercise caution while travelling in Nepal amid heavy rainfall, floods and landslides.
The embassy advised travellers to avoid visiting affected areas until weather conditions and the overall situation improve.
It urged particular caution in tourist destinations including Pisang, Chame, Manang and surrounding areas, where continuous rainfall has triggered landslides and snowfall, disrupting road connectivity in several locations. Rescue operations have also been hampered by the rugged terrain and disrupted transport links.
Authorities have suspended trekking activities in several parts of Manang, including routes to Tilicho Lake, Thorong La Pass, Ice Lake, Kang La and Bhimthang.
Travellers have also been advised to exercise caution while visiting Pokhara and surrounding areas, as landslides have disrupted road links and access to nearby trekking destinations.
Those planning to travel to Mustang, Jomsom and other mountainous areas have been advised to check road conditions in Gandaki Province, where routes can be disrupted suddenly.
Bangladeshi citizens planning trekking, mountaineering or travel in mountainous and landslide-prone areas, including Annapurna, Manang, Mustang and Manaslu, have been advised to verify travel information and strictly follow directives issued by the Nepal government and local authorities.
Bangladeshi citizens already in areas vulnerable to such hazards have been advised to stay in safe locations, avoid riverbanks and landslide-prone areas, check road and weather conditions before travelling, and remain in regular contact with their travel operators and the embassy.
The embassy said it is monitoring the situation in coordination with Nepali authorities and will issue further updates as necessary.

The incident took place around 10am on Saturday at Chand Udyan Housing in the Beribadh area of Mohammadpur.
Zainal Abedin, who described himself as a victim of the incident, submitted a written complaint to Mohammadpur police station.
According to the complaint, around 100-150 unidentified people allegedly entered the second-floor office of Mohammadpur Twin Tower after breaking its doors, locks and windows.
They allegedly searched several rooms and a storeroom before taking Tk15 lakh in cash, five laptops, two air conditioners, three CCTV cameras, office furniture and other equipment. The items were allegedly loaded onto a truck.
Zainal alleged that Md Mostak Rahman Khokon Chowdhury, 62, along with Mohin, Prince and Alamin and the assistance of several local individuals, had been attempting to take control of the office for some time.
The complaint said the incident caused financial losses to the organization and raised concerns over the loss of important official documents and information.
It further alleged that the incident disrupted the office's normal operations and caused significant financial and administrative losses.

item.title: Five arrested over attack on house in Adabor
item.description:
Five people have been arrested in connection with an attack on a house in the Shyamoli Housing area of Adabor in the capital.
Deputy Commissioner (DC) of the DMP Media and Public Relations Division, Md Akter Hossain, confirmed the matter at around 11:15am on Monday.
The DMP said five people were arrested in connection with the attack on a house in the Shyamoli Housing area of Adabor. The DMP did not immediately disclose the names or identities of those arrested.
The attack on the house in Adabor took place on Saturday morning. A group of 15 to 20 people, armed with machetes, cleavers and a pistol, allegedly carried out the attack. It has been alleged that an attempt was being made to take control of the eight-storey house.
The owner of the house, Aminur Rahman Khan, is a businessman. His nephew, Monir Hossain, said the house had also been occupied once after August 5, 2024.
Following Saturday’s incident, the house owner, Aminur Rahman, filed a case with Adabor Police Station on Sunday night.
The case names Khurshid Alam Khan, Habibullah alias Russell, Kalam, Kamran Hossain, Mizanur Rahman, Sajib Hossain, Hasibul Hasan alias Emon, Tanvir and 15–20 others as accused. The remaining individuals have been listed as unidentified.

item.title: Athlete trainer allegedly harassed at metro station over wearing shorts
The right to know
item.description:
As a nation navigating a challenging political and economic period along with seeking to rebuild its democratic foundations, access to information must be recognized as an indispensable prerequisite for accountable governance, anti-corruption, and institutional trust.
To that end, as the global community observes the International Day for Universal Access to Information under the theme "Upholding Information Integrity in the Digital Age," we must contend with some uncomfortable truths.
Historically, Bangladesh did take a progressive step with the enactment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act in 2009. Yet, the promise of that landmark legislation has been repeatedly undermined by bureaucratic resistance, colonial-era cultures of secrecy, and prolonged periods of institutional paralysis.
In our current socio-political context, institutional secrecy breeds rumours, public cynicism, and instability. At a time when disinformation and misinformation continues to grow, and technologies only amplify their reach, it is integral for everyday citizens to be empowered with the right to know and become more informed citizens.
Indeed, if citizens are to hold the government accountable for their decisions and actions, they must first know how they are governed.
To build a truly democratic society, the state must treat the right to know as non-negotiable.Digitizing public records and ensuring unhindered access to official data for citizens are critical steps in this endeavour.
Transparency has never been a threat to effective governance, and this and subsequent administrations must recognize that it is rather the strongest defense to effective governance.
On this International Day for Universal Access to Information, we hope that the authorities concerned recognize that an informed citizenry is in its best interest, and to suppress and withhold information from the public goes against any nation’s best interests.

item.title: East West University celebrates World Pharmacists Day 2026
item.description:
The Department of Pharmacy at East West University (EWU) organized a seminar titled “Empowering Pharmacists for Healthier Futures in Bangladesh” to observe World Pharmacists Day 2026 at the Manzur Elahi Auditorium on September 28.
Md Nasser Shahrear Zahedee, Chairman of Radiant Pharmaceuticals Ltd and a member of the Board of Trustees at EWU, delivered the keynote speech. Md Alamgir Hossain, Director General (Additional Secretary) of the Directorate General of Drug Administration, attended as the chief guest, while Shams Rahman, Vice Chancellor of EWU, was present as the special guest.
The program was presided over by Mohammed Farashuddin, Chairperson of the Board of Trustees and Founder Vice Chancellor of EWU. The event began with a welcome address by Amirul Islam, Chairperson of the Department of Pharmacy.
Speakers highlighted the expanding role of pharmacy in modern healthcare systems and emphasized the need for strong industry-academic collaboration to equip graduates with practical expertise, innovative thinking and ethical standards.
They said such collaboration is important for strengthening Bangladesh’s pharmaceutical industry globally, while empowering pharmacists remains vital for patient safety, drug quality and equitable healthcare services.
To mark the occasion, the department also organized two student competitions — a poster presentation and a Pharma Olympiad — followed by an awards ceremony for the winners.
The event was attended by the Pro-Vice Chancellor, Treasurer, faculty members, officials, current students and alumni of the Department of Pharmacy.

item.title: Mohammadpur gang leader Arman arrested
item.description:
Arman, known as a top gang leader in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur area, has been arrested by Special Response Battalion (SRB)-2. He is reportedly a key member of the Arman-Shahrukh gang.
Naymul Hasan, Additional DIG and Commander of SRB-2, confirmed the matter on Monday.
According to SRB sources, Arman is an accused in the recent killing of Patali group leader Forhad in Keraniganj, who was hacked and shot to death.
He is also an accused in the case filed over the killing of Alex Emon group leader Emon in Rayerbazar. Several other cases have also been filed against him with Mohammadpur Police Station.
SRB said, a machete allegedly used to hack Farhad to death, along with a foreign-made pistol and a magazine, was recovered from Arman during his arrest.
SRB will provide further details at a press briefing at its media centre in Karwan Bazar Monday afternoon.

item.title: Football Leaks and the hacker behind Manchester City’s charges
item.description:
The reported finding that Manchester City breached almost all of the 115 Premier League financial rules brought the long-running Football Leaks saga back into the spotlight — and once again drew attention to Rui Pinto, the Portuguese computer enthusiast whose disclosures helped trigger investigations into the club’s finances.
Pinto launched Football Leaks in 2015, operating under the pseudonym “John”. The self-taught computer enthusiast and former history student obtained and shared millions of confidential documents involving football clubs, players, agents and governing bodies. The material included contracts, internal emails and financial information concerning some of the biggest names in the sport.
Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, although he has also faced criminal proceedings over the methods he used to obtain information. He was arrested in Hungary in 2019 and extradited to Portugal. In 2023, he was convicted of crimes including illegal access to IT systems and attempted extortion and received a suspended prison sentence. He has since cooperated with authorities and remains under police protection.
His Football Leaks archive became a major source for investigative journalists. German magazine Der Spiegel used documents supplied by Pinto in a series of reports published from November 2018, including material concerning Manchester City’s sponsorship arrangements with companies such as Etihad and Etisalat. The revelations prompted UEFA to investigate the club’s financial affairs.
UEFA subsequently found City guilty of overstating sponsorship revenue and failing to cooperate with its investigation, imposing a two-season European competition ban in February 2020. The Court of Arbitration for Sport later overturned the ban, ruling that UEFA had not established that City had disguised equity funding as sponsorship contributions, while upholding a finding that the club had failed to cooperate with the investigation.
Pinto himself was not charged over the Manchester City material specifically. His Portuguese criminal cases concerned access to information belonging to Portuguese football clubs and other organisations.
In April 2026, Pinto was acquitted of 241 charges in a separate Portuguese case after a court ruled that the charges were invalid because they related to matters for which he had already been tried.
The latest Manchester City development is separate from those earlier UEFA proceedings. Reports on September 25 said an independent Premier League panel had found City guilty of 114 of the 115 alleged breaches. However, the Premier League has not publicly confirmed the findings, while City said its case remains ongoing and that significant elements of the process are still to be completed. The club is expected to appeal, and no sanctions have yet been decided.
For Pinto, the development represents the latest chapter in a saga that began with millions of leaked documents and has since reshaped scrutiny of financial regulation in European football.

item.title: Hasan, Khaled fire Kent back into County Championship top tier
item.description:
Bangladesh fast bowlers Hasan Mahmud and Syed Khaled Ahmed played key roles in Kent’s late-season surge as the English county side secured promotion to Division One of the County Championship.
Kent sealed second place in Division Two following the completion of their final-round fixture, earning an immediate return to the top tier after finishing bottom of the second division last season.
The contribution of Bangladesh’s two pacers was particularly significant, with Hasan and Khaled combining for 42 wickets in just seven matches during Kent’s promotion campaign.
Hasan was the first to make his mark. The right-arm pacer claimed 26 wickets in four matches before leaving the county campaign to join Bangladesh’s national team for international duty.
His spell proved especially valuable during the closing stages of Kent’s push for promotion, providing the side with a potent wicket-taking option and helping them collect crucial points.
Khaled joined Kent towards the end of the season and made an immediate impact. He took 16 wickets in three matches, including a match-winning haul of eight wickets in Kent’s seven-wicket victory over Lancashire.
That performance came at a crucial point in the promotion race and strengthened Kent’s position among the leading sides in Division Two.
Khaled maintained his form in Kent’s final match against Gloucestershire, taking five wickets across the two innings as Kent secured an eight-wicket victory.
The result completed a strong finish for Kent, but promotion was only confirmed after Northamptonshire suffered defeat against Middlesex.
Kent eventually finished second in the eight-team Division Two table with 198 points from 14 matches, while Northamptonshire ended on 191 points.
For Kent, the return to Division One marks a remarkable turnaround from last season’s last-place finish. For Bangladesh cricket, meanwhile, the campaign provided further evidence of the growing impact of its fast bowlers in overseas conditions.

item.title: Cricket Australia chair steps down after BBL backlash
item.description:
Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird announced he was standing down on Monday amid a backlash over the partial privatisation of the Big Bash Twenty20 competition.
Domestic body Cricket NSW withdrew support for Baird after Cricket Australia forged ahead with the sale of the struggling Melbourne Renegades franchise.
"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA Chair and Director," Baird said in a statement.
"I believe Australian cricket continues to be well lead by the CA Board."
Baird will leave the role after Cricket Australia's annual meeting in late October.
Cricket Australia has named former Test opener David Boon as Baird's interim replacement.
Renowned for his bushy moustache, Boon is something of a cult figure in Australian cricketing circles.
Boon's teammates once claimed he downed 52 cans of beer on a flight between Australia and England in the late 1980s.
Following his playing career, Boon has held positions as a national team selector and state cricket administrator.
"It is an enormous honour to take the role of Interim CA Chair during what is a hugely exciting and also challenging time for cricket," Boon said.
Cricket Australia has courted private investment in the domestic Twenty20 competition as it looks to shore up the game's financial future.
But privatisation has been a thorny issue.
An initial proposal to sell stakes in each of the BBL's eight teams stalled earlier this year amid concerns about a loss of control for the game's local custodians.
While the Victoria, Western Australia and Tasmania cricket associations voiced support and South Australia said it was open to the idea, New South Wales and Queensland rejected the move.

item.title: Milestone man Kohli's 139 powers India to big ODI win over West Indies
item.description:
Virat Kohli hit a record-extending 55th one-day international century after reaching 15,000 runs to lead India to a dominant eight-wicket win over the West Indies in the series opener on Sunday.
Kohli, who hit an unbeaten 139, put on 151 runs for the second wicket with skipper Shubman Gill (110) as India chased down their victory target of 296 with 50 balls to spare in Thiruvananthapuram.
Kohli hit the winning six -- the ninth in his 88-ball knock -- as India went 1-0 up in the three-match series, which is a step in the team's preparations for the 2027 ODI World Cup.
The 37-year-old Kohli made the evening his own as he went past 15,000 ODI runs to become only the second batter after icon Sachin Tendulkar to achieve the feat.
"My focus has never really been on these milestones," said Kohli.
"It's just understanding the situation along the course of just doing the job for the team. Achievements come along. Obviously, I feel very grateful and very blessed to be in this position for having played for so long."
Kohli reached the milestone with a boundary in his 303rd ODI innings, while Tendulkar, who finished his illustrious career with 18,426 runs, took 377 innings to get to 15,000.
Gill reached his 10th ODI hundred but the spotlight soon shifted back to Kohli, who reached his 100 with a six as a raucous home crowd stood up to applaud the star cricketer.
The top-order batter is leading century-maker in ODIs with Tendulkar next with 49 hundreds. Rohit Sharma is third with 34 tons.
Kohli and the 39-year-old Rohit are both playing only in the 50-over format after their Test and T20 retirements, as they look ahead to the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
"We're a year away from the World Cup. I know what my goal is, and yeah, it's pretty clear for me that whatever games we get, I just need to keep working on different aspects of the game," said Kohli.
"Keep myself physically fit, challenge myself to be out there, run from boundary to boundary in the last 15 overs if I can, field in the inner ring, show intensity."
Kohli on Saturday told broadcasters JioStar that the 2027 showpiece would be his last World Cup appearance.
Rohit got the team off to a brisk start in his 32 as he put on 74 with opening partner Gill.
Earlier, Justin Greaves made 101 and put on 135 for the first wicket with left-hander John Campbell, who made 62, to guide West Indies to 295-7.
Left-arm wrist spinner Kuldeep Yadav struck crucial blows to return figures of 4-40 including one maiden over as India hit back in the middle overs.
Kuldeep, who was named player of the match, also struck on successive balls, sending back Greaves and Jewel Andrew before Roston Chase avoided the hat-trick.
Chase steadied the innings with Amir Jangoo, who made an unbeaten 58, as the pair put on 52 for the sixth wicket.
The second ODI is on Wednesday in Guwahati.

item.title: The right to know matters more than ever
item.description:
Information has never been so abundant. Yet finding information that can be trusted has rarely been more difficult.
The scale of the problem is now global. The World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2026 ranks misinformation and disinformation as the second most serious risk over the next two years, behind geoeconomic confrontation.
The report, based on the perceptions of more than 1,300 experts worldwide, notes that technological acceleration and the growing difficulty of distinguishing authentic from synthetic content are intensifying the challenge.
Artificial intelligence has made the problem more acute. Convincing audio, video and text can now be generated and distributed at unprecedented speed and scale. Fake news cards mimicking established media outlets can be produced within minutes, while social media systems can rapidly amplify content designed to provoke fear, anger, or polarization.
The result is not simply an increase in false information; it is a deeper crisis of trust in which distinguishing fact from fabrication becomes increasingly difficult.
The WEF report warns that realistic deepfakes and AI-generated misinformation and disinformation could further fragment the public sphere and make it increasingly difficult for citizens to distinguish truth from deception.
This year's International Day for Universal Access to Information, observed on September 28, comes against precisely this backdrop. The 2026 theme -- “Upholding Information Integrity in the Digital Age: The Role of Access to Information in Addressing Information Disorder” -- highlights the importance of access to reliable information at a time when digital technologies and artificial intelligence are making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic information from false or manipulated content.
In recent years, false claims about political developments, communal violence, and government decisions, fabricated press releases and AI-generated images and videos have repeatedly circulated online. Data from Dismislab and Rumor Scanner indicate that the spread of political and religious rumours in Bangladesh increased significantly in 2024 and 2025.
This phenomenon is generally discussed as a problem of misinformation or disinformation. But there is another dimension that deserves greater attention: The availability of reliable information from authoritative sources.
When citizens cannot easily find out what a public authority has decided, how public money has been spent, or what the official record actually says, an information vacuum is created. That vacuum can quickly be filled by rumours, speculation, and fabricated narratives.
This is where the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2009 becomes particularly important.
RTI is not a fact-checking mechanism, and the Information Commission is not a fact-checking agency. Its role is different: To ensure that citizens can obtain information from authorities covered by the law, seek remedies when information is denied, and ensure compliance with the legal right to information.
But that role matters greatly in an age of information disorder. Reliable public information gives citizens something against which claims can be checked.
Consider a false claim about a government decision spreading rapidly online. One response may be to publish another statement denying it. A more durable response is to ensure that the actual decision, relevant documents, and other information are proactively available to the public. The easier it is to find the authoritative record, the less room there is for an information vacuum to be filled by falsehoods.
This makes the current state of Bangladesh's Information Commission particularly concerning.
The Commission has remained without commissioners since 2024. A five-member selection committee has been reconstituted to recommend candidates for the posts of chief information commissioner and two information commissioners. However, no subsequent appointments have been publicly reported.
The Information Commission is the institution through which citizens can ultimately seek a remedy when their requests for information are denied after the prescribed appeal process. Without commissioners, that enforcement mechanism cannot function as intended. The burden of exercising a legal right therefore falls disproportionately on the citizen.
A right is meaningful only when there is an effective mechanism for enforcing it.
Civil society organizations and research-based organisations such as Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB), along with the RTI Forum, have repeatedly called for the Commission to be made fully functional and for commissioners to be appointed through a transparent process based on competence and independence.
These demands are part of a broader reform discussion about making the right to information work effectively in practice, rather than merely guaranteeing it on paper.
But restoring the Commission alone will not resolve the weaknesses in Bangladesh's RTI regime. The law itself needs reform.
The RTI Act was an important governance reform when it was enacted in 2009. But more than 15 years later, the information environment, technology, and expectations of citizens have changed considerably. The law must therefore evolve with these realities.
The RTI (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 introduced several important changes, including provisions recognising electronic records, stronger proactive disclosure requirements, and increased penalties for certain violations. But important concerns remained. Among them was the exclusion of official note sheets from the definition of information.
The exclusion of note sheets is significant because such records can reveal how an administrative decision was processed, considered, and justified. If citizens can obtain the final decision but not the relevant record of how that decision was reached, an important part of institutional accountability remains outside public scrutiny.
The demand to include political parties as “authorities” was also not incorporated into the ordinance.
Political parties registered with the Election Commission are not currently treated as "authorities" under the RTI Act. Although registered political parties are required to submit annual financial reports to the Election Commission, citizens cannot directly seek information from political parties under the RTI framework.
This creates a gap in public accountability. Political parties participate in elections and play a central role in determining how the state is governed. Their financial transparency is therefore a legitimate matter of public interest.
Bringing political parties within an appropriate transparency framework does not mean that every aspect of their internal affairs should automatically become public. Rather, the principle should be that organizations whose activities have significant public consequences should be subject to reasonable and clearly defined transparency obligations.
Unfortunately, these important issues were not incorporated into the ordinance.
More importantly, the ordinance itself did not become permanent law. Introduced during the interim government following the July uprising, the ordinance was not enacted into permanent law after the elected government took office.
Under Article 93 of the Constitution, an ordinance ceases to have effect if it is not enacted within the constitutionally prescribed period after Parliament begins to function.
As the 13th Parliament did not pass the RTI Amendment Ordinance into law, it lapsed. The amendments it introduced therefore did not become part of the permanent RTI framework, leaving the RTI Act 2009 as the governing law.
A reform process that had introduced significant changes to the country's information-access regime therefore went back to square one.
Important changes to citizens' right to information should not remain dependent on temporary ordinances. Bangladesh needs a durable legal framework developed through meaningful consultation with citizens, journalists, researchers, civil society, and other stakeholders.
But legal reform alone will not solve the problem of information disorder.
The government must also take proactive disclosure seriously. Public authorities should routinely publish decisions, budgets, expenditure, audit reports, project information, and other information of genuine public interest in accessible and usable formats.
This is particularly important because the technology for producing and distributing false information is evolving rapidly.
The WEF report notes that distinguishing authentic from synthetic content -- whether video, audio, or written material -- is becoming progressively more difficult, while AI-generated misinformation and disinformation can amplify existing social and political divisions.
Citizens, meanwhile, need greater awareness of their right to information and greater capacity to assess information critically.
We therefore need to think about RTI differently. It is not simply an anti-corruption tool. It is not merely a mechanism for journalists to obtain documents. And it is certainly not a substitute for professional fact-checking.
It is part of the information infrastructure of an informed society.
A citizen trying to determine whether a claim about public expenditure is true should be able to find the relevant government record.
A journalist investigating a public project should be able to seek the underlying information.
A community questioning the distribution of public benefits should have a lawful means of obtaining relevant records.
And when an authority refuses information without justification, there should be an independent institution capable of providing a remedy.
For that to happen, Bangladesh needs three things at the same time.
The appointment of information commissioners should therefore be completed through a transparent process based on competence, independence, and freedom from partisan influence or nepotism.
The law should be further reviewed to address its remaining gaps, including the treatment of note sheets and the transparency of entities whose activities have significant public consequences.
Public authorities must also comply with their existing obligations to disclose information proactively.
The right to know should not depend on how persistent a citizen is, how well connected they are, or whether they can withstand the frustration of repeatedly asking an authority for information.
In an age when convincing falsehoods can be produced and distributed within minutes, access to reliable public information is part of the foundation on which citizens make sense of public affairs.
The answer to information disorder is not simply to produce more information. It is to make reliable information accessible, verifiable and accountable.
And for that, Bangladesh must make the right to know a right that works -- not merely a right that exists on paper.
Mathews Chiran is a former journalist and now works as a communications practitioner.

item.title: Why India’s opposition wants top poll official out
item.description:
The Election Commission of India, long regarded as the guardian of the world’s largest democracy, is facing scrutiny after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision.
According to an Indian Express report last week, some key decisions linked to the contentious revision exercise were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.
The ECI, a constitutional body, has rejected the allegations, saying all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.
Opposition parties have long raised doubts about the nationwide revision, which has seen millions of names removed from voter rolls, saying it benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
Here is a rundown of the major issues at stake:
The English-language daily reported that the poll body had been riven by internal disagreements since the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter lists started last year.
It said two of the ECI’s three commissioners formally lodged objections at least 14 times in the last 10 months over key SIR decisions that led to the omission of 130 million voters.
Under India’s constitution, decisions by the three-member poll body should be taken by consensus or a majority.
The ECI says the SIR exercise is intended to identify fraudulently registered voters while ensuring those who are eligible remain on the rolls.
It also says the exercise aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from voting.
But critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalized and minority communities.
Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
The ECI has denied the central allegation that decisions were taken unilaterally by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
“All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year,” it said in a statement on Wednesday.
The allegations reported by The Indian Express presented “only one part of the picture,” and “differing views” were a routine “part of decision-making,” it added.
The ECI has not publicly explained who authorized the specific orders that the two commissioners had challenged.
Opposition parties are demanding Kumar’s resignation and a Supreme Court-led investigation into the matter.
They are also seeking an independent probe into the Election Commission’s functioning as well as the voter-roll revision.
“If decisions relating to the SIR were taken without the knowledge or approval of two of the three Election Commissioners... then those decisions and the entire SIR exercise are legally invalid,” Pawan Khera of the main opposition Congress party said on social media.
“Gyanesh Kumar has done nothing short of treason.”
The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has also threatened to hit the streets from October 2 -- the birth anniversary of India’s founding father Mahatma Gandhi -- if Kumar does not resign.
The online movement, which has millions of followers on social media, forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July, following widespread student-led street protests.

item.title: Tolls mount in Thailand, Myanmar floods
item.description:
Heavy rains have killed eight people in Thailand since mid-September, the government said Monday as Bangkok battled flooding for a fourth consecutive day, with at least eight more confirmed dead in neighboring Myanmar.
The casualties in Thailand have occurred in three eastern provinces since September 16, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, with none reported in the capital.
More than 500,000 households and 1.7 million people across 27 provinces are currently affected by floods in Thailand after an intense weather system hit the region, it said.
In hard-hit Bangkok, schools were closed and authorities urged people to work from home where possible -- a call that many heeded, with roads and public transport networks noticeably quieter.
More than 80,000 people were unable to leave their homes in the capital due to flooding, the interior ministry said.
Nattapon Mankean, 32, said his apartment complex in Bang Kapi, eastern Bangkok, had no electricity or water, so he and his girlfriend fled with two cats, one in a cage and the other in a specialized rucksack.
“Our phone batteries died, we had no running water -- everything became difficult,” the 32-year-old told AFP late on Sunday.
“It was terrible, I couldn’t do anything,” he added. “I had to get out.”
Authorities declared a city-wide disaster on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain, and on Monday some residents were still wading through thigh-high waters.
In Bang Kapi locals used ice-boxes and other floating plastic containers to cart supplies from nearby markets and supermarkets, AFP reporters saw.
The rains that lashed Thailand also hit neighboring Myanmar, where rescuers said heavy floods and landslides in the southern region of Tanintharyi had killed at least eight people.
“We have recovered eight bodies while between 20 to 30 people are missing” in Launglon township, said Hein Htet, of the local volunteer group People’s Administration Team.
Three of the recovered bodies were teenagers who had gathered at a local monastery on Sunday but were swept away by a landslide that hit their village, burying 18 buildings, he said.
“There are still people and villages in the danger zone with continued rainfall,” he warned.
Myanmar’s civil war often makes the scale of natural disasters hard for humanitarian organizations to judge, as well as complicating relief efforts.
“We are inundated not only with the scale of the flood but also with the lack of resources. This is a natural disaster in the conflict area,” said Hein Htet.
September is the peak of Thailand’s rainy season, but many Bangkok residents said this year’s floods seemed worse than previous ones.
The city is built on former marshlands and is intersected by a network of canals, many of them heavily flooded by the rains.
Pumping stations have been operating at full capacity for days, but Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said Sunday it could take “up to a week” for the waters to fully drain.
Thousands of residents have decamped to temporary shelters.
In a briefing on Monday, government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said floods were receding, but “some areas in Bangkok are still facing high water levels.”
“I was so shocked, things happened so quickly,” said Samran, a retired company worker whose building was flooded.
“My flat’s car park was under water -- it never floods, even in 2011” when hundreds of people died across Thailand in heavy deluges, he said, asking AFP not to publish his family name.
“I have drinking water but I do not have water for my toilet,” he said, saying he had to use a bucket to pull water up through the window to his second-floor apartment.
Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as global warming accelerates because of fossil fuel emissions.

item.title: Trump offered to sell arms to Xi
item.description:
US President Donald Trump offered to sell arms to his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in response to concern over weapons sales to Taiwan, the US ambassador to China said in a Fox News interview that aired Sunday.
US arms sales to the self-ruled island, which China claims is part of its territory and has threatened to seize by force, have long been a thorny issue between Washington and Beijing.
The United States is required by law to supply Taiwan, which has a democratically elected president and legislature, with weapons for its defense.
US Ambassador to China David Perdue said the issue was raised again when Xi visited the United States last week.
“President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world.’ He actually asked President Xi -- would he like to buy some? -- at one point,” Perdue said in the interview.
“There are continuing conversations about other sales, (Trump) and President Xi talk about that every time they get together,” Perdue said, adding that the US position has not changed.
The White House did not immediately respond to AFP’s request for comment.
White House officials said that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, according to the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal.
The US State Department said in a statement to the New York Times that “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
The Chinese foreign ministry did not directly answer when asked about the comments on Monday, but said China has “always strengthened its national defense capabilities based on its own needs, and remains committed to maintaining world peace and stability.”
Beijing warned Taiwan in June that seeking independence “by relying on the United States or through military means is a dead end.”
Washington approved a $11.1 billion arms sale to Taiwan in December, which Perdue said was a sale of “more arms to Taiwan than any other president since 1979.”
The US paused a $14 billion weapons purchase by Taiwan in May, with Trump calling it a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China, raising fears that Taiwan’s security could be traded away.
During his Washington trip, Xi repeated his warning that Trump should show “prudence” over Taiwan, and went further to urge the United States to oppose Taiwan independence explicitly.
Both leaders confirmed they would meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November and the G20 forum at Trump’s Doral resort in Miami in December.

item.title: MTV VMAs 2026: Madonna leads with seven wins
item.description:
Madonna emerged as the biggest winner at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, taking home seven trophies at the ceremony held Monday at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
The singer, who led this year’s nominations with 13 nods, won Artist of the Year and Best Collaboration for “Bring Your Love,” her collaboration with Sabrina Carpenter.

Bangladesh issues travel advisory for tourists visiting Nepal
item.description:
NEPAL-FLOODS/

The Bangladesh Embassy in Kathmandu has urged Bangladeshi tourists and trekkers to exercise caution when travelling to areas of Nepal affected by ongoing heavy rainfall, floods and landslides.

It has also advised travellers to consider postponing trips until weather and overall conditions improve.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs shared the advisory with the media on Monday evening, citing the Bangladesh embassy.

The advisory said extra caution was necessary, particularly in Pisang, Chame, Manang and surrounding tourist areas. Continuous rainfall, landslides and snowfall have disrupted road connectivity in many places, making rescue operations difficult.

Nepalese authorities have already suspended trekking in several areas, including Tilicho Lake, Thorong La Pass, Ice Lake, Khangla and Bhimthang in Manang. Travellers have also been advised to exercise caution when visiting Pokhara and surrounding areas due to disruptions caused by landslides.

The embassy urged travellers to obtain updated information on road conditions in Gandaki Province before travelling to Mustang, Jomsom and other mountainous areas, as road access could be disrupted at short notice.

Against this backdrop, the Bangladesh Embassy advised Bangladeshi citizens to verify all relevant information before planning trekking, mountaineering or travel to mountainous and landslide-prone areas, including Annapurna, Manang, Mustang and Manaslu. They were also advised to follow instructions issued by the Nepalese government and local authorities.

Bangladeshi citizens already travelling in risk-prone areas have been advised to stay in safe locations. They were also urged to avoid riverbanks and landslide-prone areas, check road and weather conditions before travelling, and maintain regular contact with their travel operators and the embassy.

The advisory is temporary, and Kathmandu and its surrounding areas are not covered by it, the statement said.
